items.prompt: Define inventory.
items.canonical_answer: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds at a point in time: the raw materials and components it has bought but not yet used, the work in progress that has entered its process but is not yet finished, and the finished products it has made but not yet sold.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. Naming the three types completes the definition; no example or evaluation is required.

items.prompt: A manufacturer's inventory falls into three types. Identify each type, with one example of it.
items.canonical_answer: Raw materials: bought-in inputs that have not yet been used, such as timber in a furniture workshop. Work in progress: output that has entered the process but is not yet finished, such as a chassis part-welded. Finished products: completed goods not yet sold or dispatched, such as tables standing in the despatch bay.
marking_guidance: One mark-worthy point for each type correctly identified with a fitting example. No mechanism or evaluation is required.
A recall card: it asks for all three types, which the papers ask for one item at a time, so it carries no paper tariff.

items.prompt: Explain why a manufacturer may hold more work in progress than its process strictly requires.
items.canonical_answer: Some work in progress is unavoidable, because a process that takes time always has partly finished output inside it. Beyond that, a business may place a deliberate stock of part-finished output between two stages so that the later stage can keep working for a while when the earlier one stops - for a breakdown, a changeover, or a shortage of one component. The reason is continuity: without that stock, a halt at stage one idles every stage after it immediately.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is to decouple one stage from the next so a stoppage does not travel down the line.
The unavoidable minimum and the deliberate buffer must be separated.

items.prompt: Namib Bottlers sells about twice as much cordial in December as in June, but its plant and its 40 permanent staff are the same size all year. Explain how holding finished-product inventory helps it deal with that pattern.
items.canonical_answer: Because the plant and the 40 staff are fixed, matching output to sales would mean running near capacity in December and half idle in June, or hiring and releasing people twice a year. Building finished-product inventory through the quiet months lets Namib Bottlers run at an even rate all year and draw the December peak out of the store rather than out of extra capacity. The cost of that choice is the holding cost on several months of bottled cordial and the risk of it passing its date; the benefit is a steady, fully used plant and a stable workforce.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the business's own facts - a fixed plant, 40 permanent staff, December twice June.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that inventory lets output be steadier than sales.
Conclusion: must reach the choice between building stock and carrying spare capacity.

context.situation: strongly seasonal demand, fixed plant and workforce

items.prompt: A furniture workshop takes a timber delivery once a week and keeps no reserve stock of timber. Analyse the effect on the workshop if one delivery arrives two days late.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that deliveries are weekly and nothing is held back, so the week's timber is consumed by the end of the week. When the delivery is two days late the workshop runs out of material on the first of those days. The mechanism is that cutting and assembly cannot start without timber, so the machines stand and the joiners have nothing to work on; they are paid anyway, and the rent, insurance and depreciation run for those two days whether or not anything is made. The consequence is two days of output not produced, so the contribution that output would have earned is not earned, and the fixed costs of those days are carried by the remaining output. If the workshop had promised delivery dates, orders go out late. The effect on the business is a lower profit for the month and, where a customer is let down, a risk to repeat orders - which is what a reserve stock of timber is bought to prevent.
marking_guidance: Condition: weekly deliveries with no reserve stock, so the material runs out as soon as a delivery slips.
Mechanism: no timber means machines and joiners stand while wages and overheads continue.
Consequence: two days of output and its contribution are lost and orders go out late.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the profit of the business and the customers whose orders are delayed.

context.situation: weekly timber deliveries, no reserve stock

items.prompt: Explain one benefit to a hardware retailer of holding inventory of fast-moving fittings.
items.canonical_answer: It can supply a customer at once. A plumber who needs a particular elbow joint today buys it from the shop that has it, so the sale and its contribution are earned rather than lost to a competitor; and because tradespeople buy repeatedly, the shop that is reliably in stock is likely to be the one they come back to, so the benefit is not confined to the one sale.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit, not a listed one: the point must be taken through to why it matters.
The reasoning must run from the immediate sale on to repeat custom, because the developed benefit is the one that leads to a further consequence.

items.prompt: Explain one drawback of holding a large inventory of televisions in a shop with limited storage space.
items.canonical_answer: The capital is tied up and at risk. Money spent on televisions standing in a crowded store room is money the shop cannot use for anything else, and if it is financed by an overdraft it is also paying interest on it. Televisions are the wrong goods to hold for long: new models arrive, so an unsold set becomes harder to shift and often has to be discounted, and in a cramped store room the chance of damage in handling rises. The drawback therefore develops into a real loss of value, not only a delay in receiving cash.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation, not a listed one: the point must be taken through to the loss it causes.
The answer must reach obsolescence or damage, because that is what leads to the value being lost rather than merely delayed.

items.prompt: Okatana Traders holds an average inventory valued at N$450 000 and puts its holding-cost rate at 16% a year. Calculate its annual cost of holding inventory, and explain what the figure means for the business.
items.canonical_answer:
Annual holding cost = average inventory value x holding-cost rate.

Annual holding cost = N$450 000 x 0.16 = N$72 000 a year, which is N$72 000 / 12 = N$6 000 a month.

The figure is in Namibian dollars per year. It is what Okatana pays for the cover its inventory provides: the storage, the interest or opportunity cost on the capital, and the damage and obsolescence it expects. It is the amount to set against the sales it would lose by holding less.
marking_guidance: Formula must be stated before the numbers.
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: the answer is a currency amount for a period - N$72 000 a year.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the figure means for this business, namely what it is paying for the cover its inventory gives it.

items.prompt: A pharmacy in Oshakati earns a contribution of N$38 on each box of a chronic medicine and sells about 90 boxes a month. Its wholesaler delivers fortnightly. Explain why it may be worth holding more of this item than of a slow-moving cosmetic line of similar value.
items.canonical_answer: A month out of stock of the medicine costs the pharmacy 90 x 38 = N$3 420 of contribution, and the patients who need it repeat their purchase every month, so a patient who goes to another pharmacy may not come back. A slow-moving cosmetic line of similar value loses far less contribution over the same period, and the customer who cannot find it is less likely to be a returning one. Because deliveries are only fortnightly, the pharmacy cannot correct a shortage quickly. The reasoning therefore points to more cover on the medicine and less on the cosmetic, even though a rand of inventory costs the same to hold in either case.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the pharmacy's own facts - N$38 contribution, 90 boxes a month, fortnightly deliveries.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the cost of a stock-out, not the value of the item, decides how much cover is worth buying.
Conclusion: must recommend heavier cover on the medicine than on the cosmetic line.

context.situation: deciding where to concentrate inventory cover

items.prompt: Analyse the consequences for a builders' merchant of running out of cement in the middle of the building season.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that cement is a repeat purchase bought alongside other materials in the building season, when contractors are working to fixed programmes. When the yard has none, the immediate effect is that the sale cannot be made and its contribution is lost, while the yard's rent, wages and vehicle costs run as before. The mechanism that makes it worse is that a contractor who cannot get cement cannot wait: he drives to a competitor, and once he is there he buys the sand, the blocks and the reinforcing on the same trip, so the loss is not one bag but a basket. The measurable consequence is a fall in revenue larger than the cement itself, and it can persist, because the contractor now knows the competitor and may keep going there. The effect on the business is a lower contribution this season and a weakened customer base for the next one, which is the reason a merchant holds a reserve on an item like cement even though it is bulky and expensive to store.
marking_guidance: Condition: a repeat-purchase item in the season when contractors are working to programme.
Mechanism: the customer cannot wait, so the whole basket moves to a competitor.
Consequence: contribution lost on far more than the cement, with fixed costs unchanged.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the merchant's profit and its customer base beyond the single sale.

context.situation: stock-out of a staple line in peak season

items.prompt: A wholesaler with a tight cash position is considering cutting its average inventory by a third to release cash. Evaluate whether it should do so.
items.canonical_answer: It should cut, but selectively rather than across the board. The decisive criterion is not the cash released but the comparison between the holding cost saved on each line and the contribution the business would lose by running out of it. Those two amounts differ sharply line by line: a slow-moving, low-contribution item that is easy to reorder can be cut hard, while a fast-moving line that customers buy alongside everything else should be left alone, because a stock-out there costs far more than its share of the holding cost. In context, a wholesaler under cash pressure has a genuinely expensive alternative use for the money, which raises the value of releasing it and argues for acting now rather than later. The strongest argument against cutting at all is that a wholesaler sells availability as much as it sells goods: customers come because the order can be filled in full, and a business that starts short-supplying them may lose the accounts that make it viable. That is why the judgement is selective rather than a flat one-third. The condition that would change it is supplier lead time - if orders can be replenished in two or three days, deeper cuts are safe; if replenishment takes weeks, the same cut buys the same cash at much greater risk.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list of points.
Context: the answer must be argued for a wholesaler under cash pressure, whose customers value being supplied in full.
Criterion: the decisive factor is holding cost saved on each line against the contribution lost if that line runs out.
Counterargument: must address the risk to the customer accounts that availability wins.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement, such as the replenishment lead time.

context.situation: cash pressure, considering a one-third cut in average inventory
facts: average inventory to be cut by a third

items.prompt: Define buffer inventory.
items.canonical_answer: Buffer inventory, also called safety stock or the minimum inventory level, is the quantity a business plans to hold in reserve above what it expects to use during the lead time, so that usage heavier than expected or a delivery later than promised does not stop it working.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The definition must place the reserve above expected lead-time usage; no example is required.

items.prompt: A Rundu hardware store sells 50 bags of cement a day, its supplier takes 4 days to deliver, and it keeps 100 bags in reserve. Explain the difference between the store's buffer inventory and its re-order level.
items.canonical_answer: Buffer inventory is a reserve the business intends not to use, held to cover a heavier draw or a late delivery; the re-order level is the trigger at which the next order is placed. The store's buffer is its 100 bags. Its re-order level is higher, because it must also cover what the store expects to sell while the order is on its way: 50 bags a day for 4 days is 200 bags, plus the 100-bag buffer, gives a re-order level of 300 bags. So a longer delivery time would raise the re-order level while leaving the buffer unchanged.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - a reserve not meant to be used against a trigger point for ordering.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the store - a 100-bag buffer against a re-order level of 300 bags, using the formula that links them; 1 mark if the difference is asserted without the store's figures.
Boundary: reserve against trigger, linked by the formula.

items.prompt: Kavango Poultry uses 1 400 bags of feed a week, spread evenly over seven days. Its supplier's lead time is six days and it keeps a buffer of four days' usage. Calculate its re-order level.
items.canonical_answer:
Re-order level = (average usage per day x lead time in days) + buffer inventory.

Average usage per day = 1 400 / 7 = 200 bags.

Buffer inventory = 200 x 4 = 800 bags.

Usage during the lead time = 200 x 6 = 1 200 bags.

Re-order level = 1 200 + 800 = 2 000 bags.

The answer is in bags of feed. It means that when the feed store falls to 2 000 bags the next order goes in; six days later the business expects to be down to its 800-bag buffer, which the delivery should restore before any of it is needed.
marking_guidance: Formula must be stated before the numbers.
Substitution must be shown for the daily usage, the buffer and the lead-time usage.
Units: the answer is a quantity in bags, not a currency amount.
Interpretation: one sentence on what reaching 2 000 bags means the business should do.

context.situation: setting a re-order level for feed

items.prompt: Analyse what happens to a bakery's re-order level, buffer inventory and holding cost when its flour supplier's lead time rises from five days to nine, and becomes less predictable.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that nothing about the bakery's demand changes: it uses the same flour each day. The first effect is arithmetic. Expected usage while an order travels is now nine days' worth rather than five, so the amount that has to be covered rises and the re-order level rises with it - the order must be placed earlier in the cycle. The mechanism behind the second effect is uncertainty rather than length: a lead time that varies means the delivery may come several days after the usual nine, and the only protection against that is a larger reserve, so the buffer is raised as well. Because the buffer sits in the store permanently, the average level of flour held rises by the whole of that increase. The measurable consequence is a higher holding cost - more storage space, more capital tied up, and more spoilage risk on flour kept longer in a warm store - for exactly the same output sold. The effect on the business is a fall in profit caused entirely by its supplier, which is why the bakery may be willing to pay a higher price per bag to a nearer or more dependable miller.
marking_guidance: Condition: demand is unchanged; only the lead time and its variability move.
Mechanism: length raises expected lead-time usage, while variability raises the reserve needed.
Consequence: a higher re-order level, a higher buffer, a higher average inventory and so a higher holding cost.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the bakery's profit and its choice of supplier.

context.situation: supplier lead time lengthening and becoming less predictable
facts: lead time five days rising to nine

items.prompt: A Windhoek workshop imports a control board from Asia. The shipment usually takes five weeks and has arrived anywhere between four and seven weeks. The workshop fits two boards a week. Explain what re-order level it should work to.
items.canonical_answer: Expected usage while the order travels is the usual five weeks of fitting: 2 x 5 = 10 boards. The buffer has to cover the difference between the usual five weeks and the worst arrival seen, which is seven weeks - two extra weeks, or 2 x 2 = 4 boards. The re-order level is therefore 10 + 4 = 14 boards: when the shelf falls to 14, the next order goes in. The workshop's own facts drive both parts. Because the shipment is long, most of the re-order level is ordinary usage in transit; because it is unpredictable by up to two weeks, the reserve is not optional. If the workshop wanted cover against a delay worse than any yet seen, it would raise the buffer further and accept the extra holding cost, which is a judgement about how much a stopped job costs it.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the workshop's own facts - five weeks usual, four to seven weeks observed, two boards a week.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that expected transit usage and the variability of arrival are covered separately.
Conclusion: must reach a stated re-order level of 14 boards.

context.situation: long and variable import lead time
facts: observed range four to seven weeks

items.prompt: Identify what is plotted on each axis of simple inventory control charts, and what the horizontal lines drawn across them show.
items.canonical_answer: The vertical axis is the inventory level, in units of the item; the horizontal axis is time. The plotted line falls as inventory is used and rises vertically when a delivery arrives, which gives the saw-tooth shape. The horizontal lines are the maximum inventory level, the re-order level - the point at which the next order is placed - and the buffer inventory level, the reserve that should not normally be entered.
marking_guidance: Both axes must be identified with what they measure. All three horizontal lines must be stated.

items.prompt:
Rundu Bottling plots the number of crates of empty bottles it holds against the day of the month. The points below were read off that plotted line. Identify the daily usage rate, the supplier's lead time and the re-order quantity, and explain what each one tells the business.

| Day | Crates held at the start of the day | Note in the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 600 | the record begins just after a delivery, at the highest level reached |
| 1 | 2 350 | normal use |
| 2 | 2 100 | normal use |
| 3 | 1 850 | normal use |
| 4 | 1 600 | an order was placed on this day |
| 5 | 1 350 | normal use |
| 6 | 1 100 | normal use |
| 7 | 850 | normal use |
| 8 | 600 | the lowest level of the cycle; a delivery arrived at the end of this day |
| 9 | 2 350 | normal use |
| 10 | 2 100 | normal use |
items.canonical_answer:
Usage rate: the level falls 250 crates between one day and the next - 2 600 to 2 350, 2 350 to 2 100 and so on - so usage is 250 crates a day. Compared against the plan, a steady fall of this size means the assumed usage rate is holding.

Lead time: the order was placed on day 4, when the level reached 1 600 crates, and the delivery arrived at the end of day 8. That is four days, which is the lead time to set against what the supplier promised.

Re-order quantity: the level rose from 600 crates to 2 600 crates, so 2 600 - 600 = 2 000 crates were delivered.

What they mean together: the lowest point of the cycle, 600 crates, is the buffer, and the line reached it exactly as the delivery landed, so the reserve was not broken into. The business can read this cycle as running to plan, and use the three figures to check its re-order level: 250 x 4 = 1 000 crates of transit usage plus a 600-crate buffer gives the 1 600 at which it actually ordered.
marking_guidance: Comparison: each figure read off the record must be set against the plan it is meant to test - the assumed usage rate, the promised lead time, and the re-order level in use.
Meaning: each of the three figures must be interpreted, not only stated; an unread number earns nothing.
Interpretation: the answer must say that the buffer was reached but not entered, so this cycle ran to plan.

context.situation: reading one full cycle off the inventory record
facts: delivery at the end of day 8

items.prompt: A business plans on a four-day reserve and uses 50 units a day. Analyse what a delivery arriving three days after the date its inventory record planned for does to that business.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the reserve was set at four days, which is 50 x 4 = 200 units, and the plan assumed the delivery would land as the line touched it. When the delivery is three days late the line does not stop at 200 units: it keeps falling at 50 units a day. The mechanism is that there is nothing else to draw on, so the shortfall comes straight out of the reserve - 50 x 3 = 150 units of it. The measurable consequence is that the level bottoms out at 200 - 150 = 50 units, one day of cover, and the business is one further day of delay away from a stock-out that would stop production or leave orders unfilled. The effect on the business is that the protection it paid for has been spent: until the level is rebuilt it is exposed, and if this supplier is late as a habit the reserve is too small for the lead time it is actually getting, so either the buffer rises - and with it the holding cost - or the supplier arrangement has to change.
marking_guidance: Condition: a four-day reserve of 200 units, with the delivery planned to land as the reserve is reached.
Mechanism: with nothing else to draw on, the delay is absorbed by the buffer at the usage rate.
Consequence: 150 units of the 200-unit reserve are used, leaving one day of cover.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the business's exposure to a stock-out and the decision about the buffer or the supplier.

context.situation: a delivery three days later than the record planned for

items.prompt: Over three cycles, the falling line on a builders' merchant's plotted inventory record has become steeper each time, and the most recent delivery was plotted two days later than the lead time the merchant works to. Explain what the merchant should change.
items.canonical_answer: Two different figures are wrong, and the record separates them. A steeper fall each cycle means the merchant is selling faster than the usage rate it assumed, so the re-order level - which is built on that rate - is now too low and is being reached later in relation to the cover it is supposed to provide. A delivery plotted two days beyond the lead time means the supplier is slower than the figure used in the same calculation. Both push the same way, so the two errors compound: the line is falling faster and the gap it must survive is longer. The merchant should recalculate the usage rate from the last three cycles, recalculate the re-order level on the true rate and the lead time actually being achieved, and decide whether to raise the buffer or press the supplier for the delivery times it agreed. Raising the buffer is the quicker of the two and costs holding cost; fixing the lead time is slower and costs nothing if the supplier can be held to its terms.
marking_guidance: Context: must use both facts in the record - a steeper fall over three cycles and a delivery two days beyond the lead time.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the two errors compound, because the usage rate and the lead time both feed the same re-order level.
Conclusion: must reach a specific action - recalculate the rate and the re-order level, then choose between a larger buffer and a shorter lead time.

context.situation: actual line drifting away from the planned one
facts: last delivery two days beyond the lead time

items.prompt: Explain why a business's delivery promise to its own customers depends on suppliers it does not own.
items.canonical_answer: Because the order cannot be completed without every part of it. A business can control its own assembly and its own transport, but if one component is a week late the finished product is a week late, whatever the factory does. The same reasoning runs through quality and cost: a defective part reaches the customer under the seller's name, and any cost added upstream arrives either in the price the customer is charged or in the margin the business keeps. That is why the reliability of the chain, and not only the efficiency of the factory, sets what can honestly be promised.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose of the answer is to show that the promise depends on inputs the business does not control.
The explanation must reach at least one of quality or cost as well as time.

items.prompt: Explain one way in which better supply chain management reduces the amount of inventory a business has to finance.
items.canonical_answer: It shortens and steadies the lead time. A buffer exists to cover the gap between ordering and receiving, and the uncertainty in that gap; so a supplier that is nearer, delivers to a fixed schedule, and is given forecasts far enough ahead to plan lets the business hold a smaller reserve for the same protection. The saving develops twice: less capital is tied up, which can be used elsewhere or reduce borrowing, and the annual holding cost falls with the average level held. How large the saving is depends on how much of the inventory was there to cover lead-time uncertainty in the first place - a business holding stock mainly to earn bulk discounts saves little this way.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit, not a listed one: the answer must take the point through to the capital released and the holding cost saved, because those are what the shorter lead time leads to.
The size of the saving must be conditioned on how much of the inventory covers lead-time uncertainty.

items.prompt: A furniture workshop in Windhoek imports fittings from Asia through Walvis Bay. The shipment takes about six weeks, and port handling and the road haul add between three days and two weeks on top. It uses 40 fittings a week. Explain how a change of supply arrangement could cut the inventory it has to hold.
items.canonical_answer: On the present arrangement the workshop has to cover 40 x 6 = 240 fittings of ordinary usage while a shipment is at sea, and then a reserve for the part that varies - up to two extra weeks, or 40 x 2 = 80 fittings. That is more than 300 fittings standing in a store room in Windhoek, financed and exposed to damage for months. Two changes attack different halves of it. Sourcing the same fittings from a South African supplier on a weekly overland run cuts the transit usage from six weeks to one; the reserve falls too, because the variation on a road journey is days rather than weeks. Alternatively, agreeing that the importer holds the stock in Walvis Bay and releases it weekly leaves the shipping time unchanged but removes the capital from the workshop's balance sheet, at whatever price the importer charges for that service. The first cuts the inventory; the second moves it, and which is better depends on the price difference.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the workshop's own facts - six weeks at sea, three days to two weeks of variation, 40 fittings a week.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that transit usage and lead-time variability are covered by different parts of the inventory, so each needs its own remedy.
Conclusion: must reach a specific change of arrangement and say what it does to the inventory held.

context.situation: long, variable imported lead time through Walvis Bay
facts: three days to two weeks extra in port and on the road

items.prompt: A clothing retailer receives the wrong sizes from an overseas supplier twice in one season. Analyse the effect on the retailer.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the retailer buys a season's range from one supplier several months ahead and has no second source once the season has started. When the wrong sizes arrive, the immediate effect is that the rails carry stock in sizes customers are not asking for and none in the sizes they are. The mechanism is that clothing sells on availability in the right size at the right moment: a customer who cannot be fitted does not wait for a replacement shipment, because the garment is wanted now and a competitor has it. The measurable consequences follow in two directions. Sales are lost at full price during the weeks the season is worth most, and the unwanted sizes have to be cleared at a discount at the end of it, so the contribution earned on what did arrive is lower as well. The effect on the business is a season's margin damaged by a fault committed in another company, which is why a retailer of this kind may hold a second supplier, inspect before shipment, or write remedies into its contract - none of which is free.
marking_guidance: Condition: a single overseas supplier committed to months ahead, with no second source inside the season.
Mechanism: the wrong sizes cannot be sold and the right ones cannot be obtained in time, and clothing customers do not wait.
Consequence: full-price sales lost during the peak and the wrong sizes cleared at a discount later.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the retailer's margin for the season and what it does about the supplier.

items.prompt: A Windhoek vehicle assembler receives engines from South Africa twice a day, while a Katima Mulilo hardware store keeps three months of stock because its deliveries can take weeks. Explain the difference between just-in-time and just-in-case inventory management, using these two businesses.
items.canonical_answer: Under just in time, materials arrive as they are needed, so almost no inventory is held: the business minimises holding cost and accepts that a disruption reaches production quickly. Under just in case, buffer stocks are held deliberately so that a late delivery or a jump in demand is absorbed, at a higher holding cost. The assembler's twice-daily engine deliveries are just in time, and a delay at the border could stop its line within hours. The Katima Mulilo store's three months of stock is just in case, which suits a business whose deliveries can take weeks. The difference is which cost each has chosen to carry: holding stock, or being without it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark (AO1): the difference identified - which cost the business chooses to carry: holding stock or running out.
2 marks (AO2): applied to the assembler and the Katima Mulilo store, with the exposure to disruption on each side; 1 mark if only one is applied.
Boundary: the chosen cost, not tidiness or modernity.

items.prompt: Explain the purpose of holding just-in-case inventory.
items.canonical_answer: Its purpose is continuity. The stock is insurance: it is held so that production and sales carry on when a delivery is late, a machine fails, or demand is higher than expected. The reason a business pays for it is that a stoppage or a stock-out costs more than the storage, interest and spoilage on the reserve - and the price of the insurance is exactly that holding cost.
marking_guidance: Reason: the purpose is continuity when supply or demand does not behave as planned.
The answer must name the holding cost as the price paid for it.

items.prompt: A soft-drinks bottler in Katima Mulilo takes its concentrate from a plant in Gauteng, about 1 400 km away by road across one border post. Explain why a just-in-time arrangement for concentrate would be difficult for it.
items.canonical_answer: Just in time needs small deliveries arriving reliably and often, and every one of the bottler's own facts works against that. At 1 400 km the journey alone takes the best part of two days, so a daily delivery would mean a vehicle permanently on the road for one customer, which the supplier is likely to price accordingly. The single border post adds a step whose delay the bottler cannot control or predict, and a queue there on a Monday becomes a stopped bottling line on the Tuesday, because under JIT there is no concentrate in the store to draw on. Small frequent loads also lose whatever the supplier gives for a full truck. The reasoning therefore points the other way for this input: the bottler should hold a reserve of concentrate sized on how long the border can hold a load up, even if it runs its bottles and cartons - which come from nearer - much closer to just in time.
marking_guidance: Context: must use the bottler's own facts - 1 400 km, one border post, a plant in another country.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that JIT transfers the risk of every delay straight to production because nothing is held back.
Conclusion: must reach a judgement for this input rather than for the business in general.

items.prompt: A medium-sized Namibian food manufacturer is considering moving from just in case to just in time for its packaging materials. Evaluate whether it should make the change.
items.canonical_answer: It should make the change for packaging, provided it can find a supplier within a day's drive. The decisive criterion is the reliability and the distance of supply, because that is what decides whether the holding cost saved is bigger than the stoppages caused. Packaging is a favourable case in context: it is bulky, so it occupies expensive space; it is often printed to the business's own design, so it goes to waste if a label or a recipe changes; and cartons and film are made regionally rather than shipped from Asia, so a two-day replenishment is realistic in a way it would not be for an imported ingredient. The strongest argument against is that a food plant cannot run without packaging any more than it can run without food: if the cartons do not arrive, product that is already made has nowhere to go, and perishable output may be lost rather than merely delayed. That is a real risk, and it is why the recommendation is conditional rather than flat. The condition is a supplier near enough to recover from a missed delivery inside the product's shelf life, plus a small reserve of the one or two lines the plant cannot substitute; where neither can be arranged, the business should keep just-in-case cover on packaging and look for its savings elsewhere.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required, not a balanced list of points.
Context: the answer must be argued for a food manufacturer's packaging, using facts that make packaging different from other inputs.
Criterion: the decisive factor is how near and how dependable the replacement supply is.
Counterargument: must address what happens to perishable output when packaging does not arrive.
Condition: must name what the recommendation depends on, such as a supplier within recovery distance and a reserve on non-substitutable lines.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a manufacturer running just in time of a two-day delay to a single delivery of components.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is that the business holds almost no component inventory, so the material on the line is the material that arrived this morning. The immediate effect of a two-day delay is that within hours the components run out. The mechanism is that assembly cannot continue without them, so the line stands: the workforce is paid to wait, and rent, insurance and depreciation are incurred for those two days whether or not anything is made. The measurable consequence is two days of output not produced, so the contribution on that output is not earned, and it can only be recovered later if there is spare capacity to catch up - which a business running just in time, with short runs and a level schedule, often does not have. Orders promised for those days go out late, so the business may owe a penalty or lose the order. The effect on the business is a fall in profit for the period plus a risk to the customer relationship, and it is the reason the case for just in time rests on supplier reliability rather than on the holding-cost saving alone.
marking_guidance: Condition: almost no component inventory is held, so the delay reaches production within hours.
Mechanism: the line stands while wages and fixed overheads continue.
Consequence: two days of output and its contribution lost, recoverable only if spare capacity exists.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must reach the manufacturer's profit and its customers' orders.

context.situation: a single late component delivery under JIT

items.prompt: Explain one cost of adopting just in time that offsets the saving in holding cost.
items.canonical_answer: The cost of deliveries rises. Replacing monthly deliveries with weekly ones multiplies the number of journeys, and each carries a charge; a business that paid for 12 deliveries a year at N$1 500 pays 12 x 1 500 = N$18 000 before the change and 52 x 1 500 = N$78 000 after it, an increase of N$60 000 a year. The point develops because there is a second effect in the same direction: smaller orders may fall below the quantity bands at which a supplier prices keenly, so the unit cost of the materials themselves can rise as well. Neither necessarily outweighs the holding-cost saving - that depends on the amounts - but both have to be subtracted from it before the change is called a saving.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation, not a listed one: the answer must show the arithmetic so that the cost is quantified rather than asserted.
The second effect - quantity discounts given up - must be reached, because it develops the point beyond delivery charges.

items.prompt: Erindi Engineering holds an average of N$800 000 of inventory at a holding-cost rate of 15% a year and takes 12 deliveries a year at N$2 000 each. Under just in time it would hold an average of N$200 000 and take 48 deliveries a year at the same charge. Explain whether the change is worth making on these figures alone.
items.canonical_answer:
Holding cost now is N$800 000 x 0.15 = N$120 000 a year; under JIT it is N$200 000 x 0.15 = N$30 000, so the holding cost falls by N$120 000 - N$30 000 = N$90 000 a year. Delivery cost now is 12 x 2 000 = N$24 000 a year and would become 48 x 2 000 = N$96 000, an increase of N$96 000 - N$24 000 = N$72 000. The net annual saving on these figures is N$90 000 - N$72 000 = N$18 000, and average inventory falls by N$800 000 - N$200 000 = N$600 000, which is released once.

On these figures alone the change is worth making, but the reason is the N$600 000 released rather than the N$18 000 a year, which is thin enough that a single stoppage could remove it. The conclusion for Erindi is therefore that the case rests on the one-off cash and on whether its suppliers can hold to 48 deliveries; the annual saving on its own would not justify the extra exposure.
marking_guidance: Context: must use Erindi's own figures on both sides and reach the net annual saving of N$18 000.
Reasoning: the mechanism is that the holding-cost saving is partly given back in delivery charges.
Conclusion: must reach a recommendation and identify the released capital, not the annual saving, as what carries it.

facts: average inventory N$800 000 falling to N$200 000

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Just in time removes the cost of holding inventory, so it must reduce a business's total costs." Explain what is wrong with that statement and correct it.
items.canonical_answer: Two things are wrong. First, just in time reduces the cost of holding inventory; it does not remove it, because a business running just in time still holds some material and still pays for the space, the capital and the risk attached to it. Second, and more importantly, a fall in one cost is not a fall in total cost. Deliveries become smaller and more frequent, so delivery charges rise; orders may drop below the quantity at which a supplier prices keenly, so unit material costs can rise; and training, reorganisation and better quality control cost money to put in place. The correct statement is that just in time lowers holding cost and raises delivery and ordering costs, so whether total cost falls depends on which of the two amounts is larger for that business - a comparison that has to be calculated, not assumed.
marking_guidance: The error must be stated before it is corrected.
Both faults must be caught: that some inventory remains, and that one cost falling does not mean total costs fall.
A discrimination card: it corrects a stated error, which the papers do not set as a question, so it carries no paper tariff.

items.prompt: A supplier of machined replacement parts to Namibian mines is considering adopting just in time throughout its store. Evaluate whether it should apply the approach to every item it holds.
items.canonical_answer: It should not apply it to everything; it should apply it item by item. The decisive criterion is what a stock-out of each item costs, and for this business that varies enormously between lines. Its customers are mines, and a mine that is waiting for a part is losing a shift of production, so it pays for availability rather than for a keen price; a part that halts a mine is worth holding almost regardless of its own holding cost. Bar stock, fasteners and consumables are a different matter: they are used steadily, obtainable within days from a merchant in Windhoek, and cheap to replace, so running them close to just in time releases capital with little exposure. The strongest argument for going further is that just in time would also force the improvements it needs - fewer, more reliable suppliers and better information about what the mines are about to need - and those are worth having in their own right. Against that stands the fact that this business sells response time, and an approach that lengthens response time attacks the thing customers are paying for. On balance, just in time for the routine, quickly replaceable materials and a deliberate reserve on the parts that stop a mine. The judgement would change if lead times on the critical items came down to days, or if the mines moved to planned maintenance schedules shared far enough ahead for the parts to be made to order.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required - selective adoption, not a flat yes or no.
Context: the answer must be argued from this business's own situation, where customers are mines buying availability.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the cost of a stock-out on each item, which differs sharply between lines.
Counterargument: must address the genuine case for going further, namely the supplier and information improvements JIT would force.
Condition: must name what would change the judgement, such as shorter lead times on critical parts or shared maintenance schedules.

items.prompt:
Tsumeb Agri-Supplies sells fertiliser to commercial farmers. It draws 10 tonnes a day from its store, its supplier's lead time is nine days, and it holds a buffer of 60 tonnes. It orders 150 tonnes at a time. Fertiliser costs it N$9 000 a tonne and it earns a contribution of N$900 a tonne. Its average inventory is valued at N$2 400 000 and its holding-cost rate is 15% a year. Over the past two seasons the lead time has run between nine and fifteen days. The points below were read off its plotted inventory record for one normal cycle.

| Day | Tonnes held at the start of the day | What happens that day |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 210 | a delivery has just arrived |
| 3 | 180 | fertiliser being drawn from the store at the normal rate |
| 6 | 150 | the re-order level is reached and the order is placed |
| 9 | 120 | fertiliser being drawn from the store at the normal rate |
| 12 | 90 | fertiliser being drawn from the store at the normal rate |
| 15 | 60 | the buffer is reached and the delivery arrives |

Calculate the re-order level the record is consistent with, and the annual cost of holding the present inventory. Then evaluate whether the business should raise its buffer from 60 tonnes to 100 tonnes.
items.canonical_answer:
Re-order level = (average usage per day x lead time in days) + buffer inventory = 10 x 9 = 90 tonnes of transit usage, plus the 60-tonne buffer, so 90 + 60 = 150 tonnes. The record agrees: the order is placed on day 6, when the level is at 150 tonnes, and the delivery arrives on day 15 - nine days later - as the level reaches the 60-tonne buffer.

Annual holding cost = average inventory value x holding-cost rate = N$2 400 000 x 0.15 = N$360 000 a year.

What raising the buffer would cost. Forty more tonnes held permanently is 40 x 9 000 = N$360 000 more inventory, and at the same rate that is N$360 000 x 0.15 = N$54 000 a year of extra holding cost.

What it would buy. The present 60-tonne buffer is six days of usage, and the observed lead time runs to fifteen days - six days beyond the nine the re-order level is built on. So the buffer currently covers the worst delay actually seen, and covers it exactly, with nothing to spare. Raising it to 100 tonnes would add four days of cover, against delays longer than any recorded in two seasons.

Judgement: it should not raise the buffer to 100 tonnes. The decisive criterion is what the extra N$54 000 a year buys, and on the evidence it buys cover for an event that has not yet happened, while the exposure that has actually occurred is already covered. A week-long stock-out would cost roughly 60 x 900 = N$54 000 of contribution - the same as the extra holding cost - so the change only pays if a delay beyond fifteen days happens more than about once a year, which two seasons of records do not support. The strongest argument the other way is that this is a seasonal trade: a stock-out during planting costs far more than an average week, because farmers cannot delay and will not come back for the rest of the season. That argues for extra cover timed to the planting weeks rather than carried all year. The conclusion is therefore to keep the 60-tonne buffer, build a temporary reserve ahead of the planting peak, and press the supplier on the nine-to-fifteen day spread, since shortening that spread removes the problem instead of paying to live with it. This would change if the lead time became less predictable than the records show, or if the contribution per tonne rose enough to make a lost week cost materially more than N$54 000.
marking_guidance: Both calculations must be shown with formula and substitution: the re-order level of 150 tonnes and the annual holding cost of N$360 000.
The record must be used, not ignored: the day-6 order and the day-15 delivery confirm the nine-day lead time and the 60-tonne buffer.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not set out both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on Tsumeb's own figures - the observed nine-to-fifteen day spread and the N$900 contribution a tonne.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the extra N$54 000 of holding cost against the stock-out risk it removes.
Counterargument: must address the seasonal peak, when a stock-out costs more than an average week.
Condition: must name what would change the answer, such as a less predictable lead time or a higher contribution per tonne.

facts: lead time nine days, observed range nine to fifteen

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Okapuka Meat Processors packs chilled meat for supermarkets. Its cartons come from a printer in Windhoek and its casings are imported from Europe on a six-week lead time. It is considering moving to just in time across both. Evaluate the impact that adopting just in time would have on the business.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: adopt just in time for the cartons, keep a reserve on the imported casings.

Paragraph 1 - the financial impact, and its two sides. Lower average inventory means a lower annual holding cost and capital released; against that, more frequent deliveries cost more and smaller orders may lose quantity discounts. The net effect has to be calculated for each input, not assumed, and the two inputs give different answers because one supplier is 20 minutes away and the other is six weeks away.

Paragraph 2 - the operational impact. Chilled meat is perishable and has a fixed packing window, so material that is late does not merely delay output: it can spoil it. Under just in time a missed carton delivery stops packing within hours, the workforce stands, the overheads run, and the contribution on the output not packed is lost along with the meat itself.

Paragraph 3 - the impact on suppliers and staff. Fewer suppliers on longer agreements with shared schedules; the printer asked to deliver small quantities often, which costs it more and may raise the price per carton; staff trained to check quality at their own stage and to change over between runs, with more responsibility and less slack in the day.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest case for going all the way. Casings are the most expensive thing in the store and the most exposed to a change of specification by a supermarket customer, so the holding cost and the obsolescence risk on them are exactly what just in time is good at removing.

Judgement and condition: adopt for cartons, where a Windhoek supplier can replenish inside a day and the saving is real; keep a reserve of casings sized on the six-week lead time and its variability, because the cost of a stoppage on a perishable product is far larger than the holding cost avoided. Revisit if a regional casing supplier appears, or if the supermarkets begin sharing firm forecasts far enough ahead for the casings to be ordered against known demand.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: what is assessed is the structure and the point at which the judgement is reached.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is made and what it is.
Context: the plan must use Okapuka's own facts - a Windhoek printer, six-week imported casings, chilled perishable output.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the cost of a stoppage on perishable output against the holding cost saved.
Counterargument: must include the real case for applying just in time to the casings as well.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer - a regional casing supplier, or firm forecasts from the supermarkets.

context.situation: considering JIT across two very different inputs
facts: casings imported on a six-week lead time

items.prompt: Benguela Fish is a Walvis Bay processor freezing hake for export. It buys packaging from South Africa on a ten-day road lead time that has varied by up to a week, and it buys ice and cleaning chemicals locally. Its European buyers require certified traceability from catch to carton and audit their suppliers. The operations manager wants to cut the N$1 100 000 tied up in packaging inventory by moving that line to just in time. Analyse the supply chain considerations that bear on this decision, and evaluate what Benguela Fish should do.
items.canonical_answer:
The supply chain, not the store room, is where this decision is decided. Three of its features matter here. First, lead time and its variability: a ten-day road journey that has varied by up to a week means the packaging reserve is not padding, it is cover for a spread the business has actually experienced, and just in time on a line like that transfers every road and border delay straight onto the freezing line. Second, the information flow: the European buyers audit their suppliers and require traceability from catch to carton, so packaging is not a commodity that can be bought from whoever is nearest when a load fails to arrive - a substitute carton has to come from an approved, traceable source, which shortens the list of places to turn on a bad week. Third, what a stoppage costs here: hake is landed on the fishing fleet's timetable, not the factory's, so if there is nothing to pack the fish into, the raw material is already in the building and losing value while the plant waits.

Set against that, the case for acting is real. N$1 100 000 is capital standing still in a business whose working capital is consumed by fuel and quota, the holding cost runs on it every year, and printed packaging is obsolete the moment a buyer changes a label or a certification mark - which audited export customers do.

Recommendation: do not move packaging to just in time on the present supply arrangement; instead attack the lead time first and take the inventory saving as it falls. Concretely, ask the approved supplier for a fixed weekly schedule and a consignment arrangement - stock held in Walvis Bay and paid for as drawn - which removes most of the N$1 100 000 from Benguela's own balance sheet without moving the risk of the road onto the freezing line. Keep a reserve sized on the worst observed delay of a week. The decisive factor is that the cost of a stoppage is exceptionally high for this business because the raw material perishes while it waits, and no packaging saving is worth a lost landing. The strongest argument against this recommendation is that consignment stock is not free: the supplier will price the service, and part of the holding cost comes back as a higher unit price. That is the number to negotiate on, and it is why the recommendation is conditional: if the supplier's price for consignment exceeds the holding cost it removes, the better route is a second approved supplier nearer by, which shortens the lead time and makes a genuine just-in-time arrangement possible later.
marking_guidance: Both the supply chain analysis and a recommendation are required; analysis alone is incomplete.
Judgement: a specific recommendation must be reached.
Context: must use Benguela's own facts - the ten-day varying lead time, the audited traceability requirement, and the N$1 100 000 tied up.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the cost of a stoppage where the raw material perishes while the plant waits.
Counterargument: must address the price the supplier would charge for holding consignment stock.
Condition: must state what would reverse or advance the recommendation, such as a nearer approved supplier.

context.situation: considering JIT on an imported packaging line
facts: ten-day road lead time varying by up to a week
buyers audit suppliers and require traceability
hake landed on the fleet's timetable

items.prompt: A new operations manager has to decide how much of each item her store should carry. Identify the questions she should ask about an item before deciding, and explain what each one tells her.
items.canonical_answer:
What is this item for - is it a raw material, work in progress or a finished product? Raw materials are held to keep the process running between deliveries; finished products are held to supply a customer immediately and to let output be steadier than sales. The answer tells her which risk she is buying cover against.

How fast does it move, and how predictably? A steady, well-forecast draw can be cut close; a lumpy one cannot, because the same average hides weeks that empty the shelf.

How long does replacement take, and how much does that vary? Both parts matter separately: the usual lead time sets how much will be used while an order travels, and the variability sets the reserve on top.

What does it cost to hold? Space, the capital tied up, and the risk of it deteriorating or going out of date while it waits. A rand of chilled goods or of fashion stock costs far more to hold for a month than a rand of sand.

What does it cost to be without it? The contribution on the sales that would be lost, the cost of a stopped process, and whether a customer turned away comes back. This is the figure most often left out, because no invoice arrives for it.

Is anything else bought alongside it? An item customers buy as part of a basket is worth more cover than its own margin suggests, because running out of it can move the whole basket elsewhere.

Taken together, these questions tell her that the right level is set item by item: hold more where being without it is expensive and holding it is cheap, and less where the reverse is true.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what a particular answer would mean for the level chosen.
Context: the answer must treat each item separately rather than setting one policy for the whole store.
The cost of being without the item must appear, not only the cost of holding it.

context.situation: setting inventory levels item by item
